j01:
Until that’s happened, the group is still a circle of promising strangers, and I wouldn’t ask that circle to take on a mortgage yet. In the meantime there’s plenty to do! Meet in rented or borrowed space, or at someone’s house, and find out how much conflict the group can handle before anyone hires a surveyor.

Along with that, you'll also need a budget of what the group can provide on the practical side. That is, the things they can offer in the way of water, housing, food stores, health care, tools, seasonal labor, transportation, schooling, market access, etc. If there are outside debts to pay or cash reserves, how long will the cash last? What are the few critical skills that could stop everything if nobody had them? It's boring stuff, I know. But in the end, a group could be great on an emotional level but be dead in the water because the well fails, or because one exhausted person is the only one who knows where everything is and how it works.

Please Choose the Values Before Falling in Love With the View

Have you noticed people often choose their community in the same way they would choose a vacation rental? “Wow! Look at this beautiful land! And a pond, with the sunset in it!! Who needs a beach?! And the people seem really nice, let’s get in here!” Fast forward two years. “Wait, there’s a vaccination policy?? And you need paperwork for it?!?!”

When you go to visit a community, have a list ready of what you really believe about children, money, property ownership, romance, medicine, food, spiritual practice, technology, privacy, conflict and leaving. Long list, huh? Mark the places on it where you're still unsure, too.

Throw sexuality and gender onto that list. Could an LGBTQ+ member live openly there? Date and/or be in a relationship? Would the community keep them fully protected? Should children be taught to question their sexual identities at an early age? Should one of the children grow up to be gay or transgender, what happens then? Until a group has answered these questions, its values on freedom and child-rearing are incomplete. Both of them!

Willing to experiment? That's a real value too! Make sure that your list declares whether or not you value experimenting, because the folks next to you may think experimenting ended in 1978 and anything that came from it is doctrine now.

Once you’ve got a good sense of what is important to you, compare this to how the group actually functions (not just how they talk about it in public). How was a recent conflict handled? Who can block decisions? How did it go for the last person who left the group? Who owns the land? It’ll be uncomfortable to have these conversations, but the view won’t go away after you’ve had them.
j02:
When Somebody Has to Go

A community that wants to be safe can't promise to keep everyone. Yeah, that's pretty tough, but sometimes somebody's gotta go. It can be the right thing to eject someone when they're a serious or generalized danger to others, repeatedly violate essential boundaries, or are just impossible to live with. If restorative work can work with the person in question in a reasonable amount of time, all the better. But if the person is endangering everyone else, the community shouldn't have to serve as a treatment program for them.

But the power to remove people is also one of the easiest to abuse. So work out the process before it's about anyone in particular. What will constitute cause for immediate action to protect people? Who will decide whether to put temporary restrictions on someone? Who will ensure that evidence is preserved? Who will be recused? How will the person be able to reply to the concerns and have the decision reviewed or appealed, without putting anyone in danger? How will their interests in housing, records, family contact, access to common resources or outside funds (if any) be protected during the separation? When will outside help be sought? (More on that next.)

'Outside' doesn't always mean the nation-state. My research initially leaned too far that way. What's really needed is that there be a competent layer that isn't reviewing its own conduct. That can be another community, a federation, a professional, an autonomous regional institution, a court, a regulatory agency, an emergency service. Just not whoever's being reviewed! The Zapatistas are an important correction here: autonomous institutions can review local power without becoming the state, and when power crept up in their own system, they pushed it back down. But autonomy doesn't mean that anyone can erase non-waivable individual rights, or that outside jurisdiction disappears.

Also agree on a mediator or ombud in advance. Why bother? People often do not trust someone who they have not met, and who appears at the time of a crisis to act as a ‘neutral stranger’. Remember that mediation is about trying to restore good relations between people. It does not remove the need for evidence, for safeguarding, for a ruling, or for a final separation when consent to continue in a shared life is no longer present.
